case_study_insert.main_stem: Sunfield Retreats (SFR) is a public limited company in the leisure and hospitality sector, running wellness resorts and glamping sites and employing a workforce of 42. Founded in 2008 by Priya Raman, SFR uses a hierarchical organisational structure with democratic leadership, so area managers consult resort teams before changing guest services. SFR plans to invest $1,200,000 in a new wellness spa and 40-unit glamping site, financed by a $700,000 ten-year bank loan, a $300,000 share issue and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $30 a unit and a selling price of $110, and currently produces 14,000 units a year, each a booked guest-night. SFR faces two problems: staff turnover has reached 14% and maintenance complaints about the cabins are rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Operations Report — Q1 2025: SFR hosted 3,500 guest-nights in the quarter at an occupancy of 69%, down from 76% a year ago. Maintenance complaints rose to 52 per month from 31. Review score fell to 3.9 from 4.4 out of 5. Average check-in wait is 9 minutes. A survey of 700 guests found that 66% would pay up to $12 more for a wellness package and 58% prefer eco-friendly cabins. Records show 15 of 42 staff have not completed on-the-job training in cabin maintenance; off-the-job training certification costs $340 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Sunfield Retreats as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Leisure Bulletin (August 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.50%, raising finance costs on SFR's variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $13.00 to $13.92 per hour, lifting the wage bill for SFR's 42 staff. (3) Resort energy and maintenance input costs have risen 10.6% year-on-year, while staycation spending grew 3.9% and regional tourist arrivals rose 4.6%.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for SFR of raising the $300,000 through a share issue rather than increasing the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $300,000 share issue brings in equity that carries no interest or repayment schedule, so SFR avoids adding to the interest burden on its $700,000 loan while developing the $1,200,000 spa and glamping site. With fixed costs of $240,000 a year already to cover, avoiding extra debt service protects cash flow. The new shareholders also share the risk: if the 40 glamping units are slow to fill, SFR is not obliged to find fixed loan instalments.

Point 2: Equity can be a larger and more flexible source than borrowing, allowing SFR to proceed with the whole development now rather than delaying it. The $200,000 retained profit stays available for working capital, which matters because trade receivables have risen to $130,000 in Appendix 2. As a public limited company SFR can access investors more easily, and keeping the loan at $700,000 leaves room to borrow later if the 14% staff turnover demands extra spending on recruitment.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of a share issue over more debt identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to SFR's $1,200,000 development, debt and cash position.

questions.question_text: SFR is launching the new wellness spa and glamping site. Consider national television advertising, regional press advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should SFR choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: TV would give the spa and glamping launch huge reach and could quickly build brand recognition for SFR as a public limited company. The production and airtime costs, however, are very high for a business servicing a $700,000 loan, and most viewers are too far away to book a stay. With occupancy at 69%, SFR needs cost-effective bookings rather than broad awareness.

Regional press advertising: Newspapers and magazines in SFR's regions are cheaper and can target nearby staycationers, with scope for detailed pictures of the 40 glamping units. Their reach is limited and print readership is falling, so they cannot by themselves generate the 14,000 guest-nights a year needed, and the message lacks the visual impact of video.

Social media influencer marketing: Wellness and travel influencers can demonstrate the spa and eco-friendly cabins to the 58% of 700 surveyed guests who prefer such cabins, and the 66% who would pay $12 more for a wellness package. Engagement is measurable and can be targeted nationally. It builds results more slowly than TV and depends on influencer fit, but cost per booking is low.

Recommendation: SFR should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the exact segments in the survey, supports the $12 premium and scales beyond regional press at a fraction of television cost. Television is rejected as too expensive and geographically wasteful, and regional press is rejected as too small to lift occupancy from 69% and justify the $1,200,000 development. SFR can also reuse influencer footage in its own booking app.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the three promotional options with minimal reference to SFR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of at least two options with some application to SFR's launch and occupancy.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options with a justified recommendation explaining why television and regional press are rejected.

questions.question_text: SFR's staff turnover has reached 14% and maintenance complaints are rising. Explain two benefits for SFR of using democratic leadership to improve staff motivation.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites SFR's 42 resort employees to contribute ideas on cabin maintenance and guest services, which satisfies social and esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Staff who help set maintenance routines are more likely to spot faults early, directly attacking the 52 complaints a month and protecting the 3.9 review score. In a hierarchical structure, consulting teams also gives area managers practical information before they change service standards.

Point 2: Involvement increases commitment and should reduce the 14% staff turnover, saving repeated recruitment and the $340 per employee certification cost. Stable, motivated staff protect the 3,500 guest-nights handled last quarter and the $80 contribution on each, which is vital while the $700,000 loan is being repaid and the new glamping site needs experienced teams. Consultation also suits a public limited company accountable to shareholders, because lower turnover cuts the cost of replacing 42 staff and protects the $80 contribution.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of democratic leadership identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to SFR's turnover, complaints and training costs.

questions.question_text: SFR must train 15 staff in cabin maintenance procedures. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training with certification. Which should SFR choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training alongside experienced maintenance staff is specific to SFR's own cabins, costs no fees and keeps all 15 employees productive while they learn. This directly targets the 52 monthly maintenance complaints and protects the 3,500 guest-nights sold last quarter. Its weaknesses are that trainers are also working, so response times may slow, and informal habits can be passed on; without certification, guests may question whether standards are verified.

Off-the-job training: Certification costs $340 per employee, so 15 staff cost $5,100 — modest against the $1,200,000 development — and gives structured, recognised maintenance skills. It removes 15 of 42 staff from the resorts while occupancy is only 69%, cutting capacity, and generic course content may not match SFR's glamping units, so on-site follow-up would still be required.

Decision: SFR should choose on-the-job training with short certification top-ups for senior staff. It is cheaper, cabin-specific and avoids losing 15 workers while complaints are high; full off-the-job training is rejected because the capacity loss and $5,100 fee are less justifiable than practical training on the units the staff actually maintain. Area managers should inspect cabins weekly while training runs so the 52 complaints do not rise, and any trainee below standard should be paired with a senior colleague. If certification is later required, $5,100 can be spread across the year from retained profit rather than from the working-capital buffer, keeping the 3,500 guest-nights and the 3.9 review score stable while the 40 glamping units open and 69% occupancy is defended for the public limited company.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to SFR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of SFR's maintenance problem.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance to SFR's cabins.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how SFR's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $240,000 ÷ ($110 − $30) = $240,000 ÷ $80 = 3,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 3,000 guest-nights a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $110 − $30 = $80. Answer: contribution per unit is $80.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways SFR's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare 3,000-unit break-even with actual output of 14,000 guest-nights: the margin of safety is 11,000 guest-nights, showing the new 40 glamping units can be phased in safely.
2. Use the $80 contribution to test the wellness premium: adding the $12 guests said they would pay gives $92 a guest-night, which can be weighed against the 66% of 700 surveyed guests who support it.
3. Check financing capacity: only 3,000 guest-nights are needed to break even, so the $700,000 loan and $300,000 share issue can be serviced; managers can set monthly occupancy targets accordingly.
4. Benchmark unit cost: $240,000 ÷ 14,000 units + $30 = $47.14 a guest-night, a figure to monitor each quarter so the 10.6% maintenance-cost inflation is spotted before it erodes the $80 contribution.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 3,000 guest-nights | (ii) Contribution per unit = $80 | (iii) Four uses: 11,000-guest-night margin of safety, $12 wellness-premium modelling, loan/equity feasibility and $47.14 unit-cost benchmarking.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SFR's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has SFR's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.25 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.35 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.92 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.11 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $40,000 inventories + $75,000 trade receivables + $35,000 cash = $150,000. 2025 current assets = $34,000 + $130,000 + $25,000 = $189,000. 2024: $150,000 ÷ $120,000 = 1.25; 2025: $189,000 ÷ $140,000 = 1.35. Excluding inventories: 2024 ($150,000 − $40,000) ÷ $120,000 = $110,000 ÷ $120,000 = 0.92; 2025 ($189,000 − $34,000) ÷ $140,000 = $155,000 ÷ $140,000 = 1.11.

Evaluation: Liquidity improved on both measures. The first rose from 1.25 to 1.35 because current assets grew faster than current liabilities, which moved from $120,000 to $140,000. More importantly, the second rose from 0.92 to 1.11, so SFR is no longer dependent on selling inventories to meet short-term obligations — valuable when $1,200,000 is committed to a spa and glamping site. However, trade receivables climbed from $75,000 to $130,000 and cash fell from $35,000 to $25,000, so much of the improvement sits in balances that may be slow to collect; credit control is needed before the group relies on that cash.

Conclusion: SFR's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher and the acid test now exceeds 1, showing genuine short-term strength. The caveat is the large rise in receivables, which should be controlled while the new development absorbs cash. The $200,000 retained profit committed to the spa should be rebuilt before further borrowing, since cash of $25,000 is thin against a $700,000 loan.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years plus detailed evaluation of receivables, cash and liabilities and a justified conclusion on improvement.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for SFR of introducing wellness packages priced up to $12 above the normal room rate.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 700 guests found that 66% would pay up to $12 more for a wellness package and 58% prefer eco-friendly cabins. A $12 premium would lift contribution from $80 to $92 a guest-night, helping cover the $240,000 fixed costs and the interest on the $700,000 loan. It also raises the appeal of the 40-unit glamping site and could lift the 69% occupancy rate.

Disadvantage: Delivering Wellness services adds staffing and equipment costs that may not be fully captured in the $30 variable cost, so the $12 premium could be eaten by higher costs. If guests judge the service poor, the review score of 3.9 could fall further and the 52 maintenance complaints might rise, undermining the $1,200,000 investment in the new spa. A stronger wellness offer may also attract the 58% who prefer eco-friendly cabins, helping fill the 40 new units, raise 69% occupancy and supporting the $80 contribution.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development using SFR's survey, costs and investment.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.50%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 10.6% rise in energy and maintenance costs will affect SFR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.50%): If SFR's $700,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra interest is 0.75% of $700,000 = $5,250 a year (0.0075 × $700,000). That is a manageable sum beside fixed costs of $240,000 a year and would be zero if the loan were fixed. Higher rates may also soften staycation demand, but the direct cost can largely be removed by refinancing.

Minimum wage increase (7.1%, to $13.92 per hour): SFR has a workforce of 42 across its resorts, so the rise raises the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert does not state hours worked or individual pay, so a defensible annual total cannot be invented; the proper test is productivity of 14,000 guest-nights ÷ 42 staff = 333.33 guest-nights per worker. If that is maintained the rise is spread across output, but with 14% turnover disruption it could push up unit labour cost and cut the $80 contribution.

Energy and maintenance inflation (10.6%): The $30 variable cost per guest-night is not broken down in the insert, so only a bound is honest: if the whole $30 rose 10.6%, that is 0.106 × $30 = $3.18 a guest-night, and at 14,000 guest-nights roughly $44,520 a year. It hits every booking and directly threatens the contribution that supports the $1,200,000 development, although the $12 wellness premium can offset part of it.

Conclusion: The 10.6% rise in energy and maintenance costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 14,000 guest-nights and erodes the $80 contribution, whereas the interest rise is a bounded $5,250 and the wage rise can be absorbed if 333.33 guest-nights per worker is sustained.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to SFR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on SFR's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in SFR's context with a justified greatest-impact judgment and reasons why the others are smaller.
